thread.title: A Handful Of Stocks That Beat The Market By 11% Over 6 Months

title: A Handful Of Stocks That Beat The Market By 11% Over 6 Months
text:
A Handful Of Stocks That Beat The Market By 11% Over 6 Months Jan. 25, 2018 1:20 PM ET | 
My initial portfolio to supplement index funds has done very well. 
The strategy is to keep a focused group of high-potential, limited-downside stocks. 
Am I good or just lucky? It's too early to tell. Discipline is the only way to improve long-term results. My journey to stock picking started with a total commitment to index funds. For 10 years I followed a simple plan with no attempts to predict what would happen to the markets or individual companies. It worked beautifully. Then last year I decided my assets were large enough to earn a significant return if I found better investments. At the same time I placed a much higher priority on being able to work on my own terms at all times. Investment research is one of the paths I pursued to let me work more independently and earn a better return on my capital. It's pretty close to what I enjoy doing anyway and doesn't require answering to anyone! It won't be enough to live off of at this point. But a faster rate of growth will get me there sooner. At the same time I'm starting some new businesses built around a high return on capital so my research will hopefully give me more ideas to run those well. And the lessons from my businesses may help me analyze stocks. Top Priority: Growth My biggest, and only, priority is to maximize long-term growth of my assets. I don't expect any income since I make other liquidity arrangements. If I need to wait a few years for something to resolve itself in order to earn a higher profit, I'll take that. I am hoping to earn a compound return of at least 15% per year on my individual stock picks. If I were willing to settle for 7 - 8% I would just buy a few index funds and ignore them (this is still the largest part of my portfolio). Given the growth focus I keep these stocks in a TFSA account, the Canadian equivalent of a Roth IRA, to minimize taxes for the rest of my life. However a large loss would mean I have to give up that benefit. So I have to maximize growth while minimizing risk. If everything goes well after a couple of decades I could have millions of dollars in assets creating tax-free growth and income. That's enough to boost the already-exceptional level of financial freedom I enjoy. The Portfolio These are the holdings I started off with. I track all results in Canadian dollars, which have not changed much against the USD over this period. The majority of these positions were bought in late July with a large addition to Home Capital in early September and a smaller addition to Shopify in October. That means the portfolio is about 6 months old and hasn't changed much along the way. For most of these positions I have bought and waited. I don't expect to do much short-term trading. Home Capital is the one I'm most likely to sell in 1 - 2 years if the share price rises enough. The others would take an extreme overvaluation to force me out. If I see a doubling in 5 years, or get 5x in 10 years, that would be a good result. A typical index fund mix is more likely to double in about 10 years on average. I am hoping to see a large drop in the price along the way so I can buy a lot more shares. Part of my reason for buying these shares now was so I can be sure not to miss that drop if it happens! I can create a spreadsheet tracking hundreds of stocks on a watchlist but losing money has a way of focusing my attention. Home Capital Group ( OTCPK:HMCBF ) +28.5% HCG (as it's known on the TSX) is my largest position by far. I started with a small options trade that earned a 450% profit, buying at a lower price than Warren Buffett and getting out near the top last summer. The timing was more luck than skill. The danger with options is that you can lose money even if you're right. So I transitioned to direct ownership of a handful of shares when the price fell back in July, then held my breath and took a much larger position ahead of an important shareholder vote in September. With the next earnings release I was rewarded with a quick gain. I expect the price could easily rise into the 20s this year. Reinstatement of the dividend would be a major positive. The biggest risk is credit losses if the Ontario housing market collapses but it appears stable at the moment. I plan to hold the shares until the price passes the book value or significant economic challenges come up. If nothing changes for a year I'll reevaluate my position. I'd be happy to sell the shares at a good premium to the book value (maybe 1.3 - 1.5x). On the other hand HCG has been a target of short sellers for a long time who want to see a Canadian housing bust. If they keep up their attacks, the price might rise to around the book value and no higher. Combined with healthy profits the company might deliver a good dividend yield and modest price growth. I would consider holding some of the shares for the long term in this scenario. Amazon ( AMZN ) +32.1% Large companies are usually not the place you look for high growth, and Amazon is one of the largest in the world. It is also an exceptional company that has been driven for over 20 years by smart decisions by Jeff Bezos. Now those decisions seem to be embedded in a company-wide culture. I think there's a very good chance of more growth ahead for Amazon. It's rare that a company comes along with a shot at being as dominant as Standard Oil was. Amazon might actually do it. The heavy reinvestment behind that growth masks actual profits so it's hard for outsiders to tell what's happening. I look to growth in the operating cash flow, which has surged in the last few years, to show that the company is creating value. Recent prices are around 40x that cash flow level. If the company sees a few more years of good growth this looks like a reasonable price. Even if the company goes through a repeat of the dot-com crash (where the price fell a lot before recovering) I would be happy with the long-term results. If it looks like the company is running out of room to expand I'll reevaluate my position. Shopify ( SHOP ) +30.2% At first I thought Shopify was just another over-hyped IPO. The turning point was when I saw that their revenue for each subscriber cohort actually grows over time. A subscription business bases its profitability on customer retention. Growing revenue per subscriber is the gold standard that very few can ever reach. Seeing that along with the high ROI and growth rates was enough to convince me. The short attack in October gave me a chance to buy more shares around the same price as my first purchase. If it looks like the growth rate is being reduced permanently I'll reevaluate my position. At the moment the management is achieving one of their highest growth rates ever so the future looks promising. Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A )( BRK.B ) +23.8% I've admired Warren Buffett for a long time. I've also admired his advice that non-professional investors should stick to index funds. When I looked around I saw that the shares were trading at a price-to-book ratio of around 1.4. Since Buffett has stated that a ratio of 1.2 would be so cheap that he is forced to buy back shares, this seemed like a reasonably good price and I bought a small position. I would like to see the price fall so I can add to the position. The stock has disappointed me thus far. Twilio ( TWLO ) -6.4% I bought a small position in Twilio without doing much research. The stock seemed beaten down but I know the business is good. A quick scan of their financial statements showed that continued growth should justify the price comfortably. I did this to see if the stock will recover in a year or two when the bad news is forgotten. So far it's gone the other way. I considered selling the position but I want to keep watching this and see what happens! Netflix ( NFLX ) +37.7% One of my inspirations for doing more stock research was a friend who retired largely on the strength of his Netflix stock returns. Obviously I can't go back and buy it 10 years ago. However the company still seems to be growing quickly. It evolved from mailing DVDs to online streaming, and now it's evolving from licensing content to creating its own content. If that goes well it could have a much larger future value. I bought a small position and I'm hoping I'll see better prices. So far it's been a total failure on that metric! Priceline ( PCLN ) +6.0% I picked up on the strength of Priceline's growth from an article in The Economist. A lot of businesses can grow their earnings and assets, but issue a lot of new shares in the process. The average shareholder doesn't benefit much. Priceline is different -- it has created very large growth in per-share earnings since the early 2000s. Managers who can do that are worthy of an investor's trust. At $2000/share it's not a cheap stock to buy as an experiment. But it will make it easy to see if the price falls. Since it seems like a strong business that would be a great buy-in point for more. Fairfax ( OTCPK:FRFHF ) +13.6% Fairfax has a structure modeled on Berkshire Hathaway which gives it some natural advantages. The long-term return is comparable to what Warren Buffet has produced. The last 10 years are where the risk lies though. A successful bet on the US housing bubble was followed by an unsuccessful bet on a Canadian housing bubble and a disastrous stock market hedge that wiped out all the investment gains from 2010 - 2016. I just don't understand the logic of buying stocks while betting that the stock market will crash. If it's a 100-to-1 payoff (like the deflation swaps that the company still holds) that's one thing. But wiping out all your gains when you're wrong is pure overconfidence. On top of that the company faced big insurance payments in 2017. All of this combined brought the price-to-book ratio down and gave me a healthy entry point. I think this has the potential for long-term returns similar to Berkshire Hathaway. It's also much smaller and more involved in fast-growing emerging markets. The bad bets are a downside. I bought in after they were unwound. If there are more bets like that I may get out. Results Well Above The Market I started my portfolio with a few top picks at the end of July, and added some more in early September. The results of the first 6 months have been very strong. The majority of my assets are still in a mix of index funds (as well as one real estate investment that is entirely managed by someone else so it's just about as passive). This provides a good comparison. In that time the rest of portfolio had a return of 14.1%. My individual stock picks earned a return of 25.1%, beating the passive investments by 11% in 6 months. I measure the total P/E ratio of the portfolio. For some of the stocks I also estimate "normalized" earnings. For example Home Capital will clearly have higher earnings as it recovers, while Amazon and Shopify would have higher earnings if they weren't reinvesting so much. In the cases of companies based on depreciation and cash flow (REITs and shipping companies) I use a number closer to the operating cash flow for adjusted earnings. The total P/E ratio of the portfolio is 27.6, but with the adjusted earnings it's only 12.9 (including the new additions discussed below). This is well below the P/E ratio of all major stock indexes, a good sign that even in a recession or bear market they may hold up their value better than the index. And if the managers allocate their profits well I should see very good growth. Measuring precise returns can be hard. If there's one thing worse than losing money, it's not knowing that you're losing money. Inspired by David Einhorn's book Fooling Some Of The People All Of The Time , I'll be using monthly snapshots to let me look up all of the past details. This will let me share exactly how the portfolio is doing. Increasing Caution Anyone can get lucky over the short term. The 90s were full of day-traders who made triple-digit gains and then lost it all. How do I know I'm not one of them? Only time will tell. Seeing gains across the board in such a short time tells me that I need to be increasingly cautious. I plan to keep a disciplined strategy, and not take long shots in hopes of a big return. The math does not work in your favor unless you get lucky and then get out. I want a strategy I can use for the long term without counting on luck. It's much better to buy stocks that show signs of delivering value well above their price while also having 2 or 3 ways to protect your investment if things go wrong. Good ideas aren't enough either. It also takes good portfolio management to turn those ideas into profits, not waiting too long to get into the right stocks or holding onto the ones that have run out their potential. This is the biggest piece I need to learn. The simplest choice is to never sell and I like stocks that support this option. Margin Call , perhaps the greatest financial movie of all time, has a good line: "There are only three ways to make money in this business. Be first, be smartest, or cheat. Now I don't cheat, and for all of the smart people we have here I think it a lot easier to just be first." I place a premium on acting before it's too late. That means the opportunity has to be good enough to mitigate the risk of being wrong. Changes To The Portfolio I want to make this portfolio public so I can talk about the future returns without looking like I just selected the good investments (it already looks like that since I've had good luck so far). I have bought a handful of other stocks in the last 6 weeks with a total value that's around 40% of the holdings above. Some are inspired by analysis on Seeking Alpha or examples shared by other great investors. I consider these to be more experimental -- I'm buying smaller positions to see what happens and learn about the industries. There are some that I would consider a part of the core portfolio. I believe in their potential enough that I'm willing to bet they return more than the index over the next 5 - 10 years. I want to list them here to avoid the temptation of only selecting the ones that did well when reporting future results! They are: Air Canada ( OTCQX:ACDVF ), Cenovus ( CVE ), Fiat Chrysler ( FCAU ), GM ( GM ), Delta ( DAL ), Southwest ( LUV ), Aercap ( AER ), Apple ( AAPL ), Facebook ( FB ), Google ( GOOGL ), and Fairfax India ( OTCPK:FFXDF ). I've already bought each of these with returns to date ranging from -9.9% (Air Canada) to +29.1% (Fiat Chrysler) On some of these I know I'm late to the game but I want to see what happens so I intentionally kept the positions small. I believe the tech companies are the ones with the clearest potential for further growth relative to their price. Their position is so strong that they may be nowhere near their limits. These, as well as a handful of other experiments, make for a lot of stocks to watch. I'll keep investigating each of them and some other ideas I haven't bought yet. When I see good potential combined with good pricing I'm ready to go for larger positions. I expect the number of large positions to be much less, no more than 5 - 10. I don't need to buy every good stock. I want to focus on only the best and invest a lot in them. If the results I see give me more confidence in my ability to find stocks with high long-term returns, I'll continue shifting more of my portfolio into them. Disclosure: I am/we are long ALL OF THE ABOVE. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article. Additional disclosure: I own all the stocks listed here. I may add to my positions or sell them at any time without notice. I do not make any representations about my views in the future.
